newsitem.title: INDIA: India should expand commodity futures - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: India should expand commodity futures - World Bank.

text.p: The World Bank has said that India should expand futures trading to cover more commodities in order to reduce risks arising from price fluctuations and spur agricultural growth.

"Revitalising and expanding its futures market is a viable option for India to help mitigate against risks, uncertainty and price volatility inherent in a more open and liberalised agricultural sector," the bank said in a study, the summary of which was obtained by Reuters on Wednesday.

In the study, jointly conducted with the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the Indian government, the bank said futures trading could help India if a large part of the physical trade was left to private firms.
At present India allows futures trading only in castorseed, hessian, gur (jaggery), potatoes, turmeric and pepper.
An official committee has recommended futures trading in cotton, oilseeds, silver, gold and sugar.

India's international pepper futures exchange is scheduled to start functioning in April. It also has plans to set up a global castor oil exchange futures and revive domestic futures in cotton and jute.
The government should play an important role in providing a stable foreign trade environment, the report said.
The bank said price volatility was becoming a major concern in the country, where the agriculture sector employs more than 60 percent of the work-force.
The bank said price fluctuations created uncertainty and risks that could threaten agricultural performance and affect the income and welfare of farmers and the rural poor.
"Futures markets provide a market-based mechanism for managing price risks which can help India create a more competitive and level playing field for commodity trade..," the bank said.
The bank said reintroducing domestic futures in cotton would be highly favourable in the short run, but immediate prospects for cottonseeds and yarn appeared dim.
It said in the oilseeds industry, futures contracts facing little competition from abroad would stand a greater chance of success.
The bank said groundnut, rapeseed and mustard futures contracts stood a greater chance of success than soybean contracts which would have to compete with foreign futures markets.
